This work investigates the characteristics of heavy-heavy hadronic clusters, which are hypothesized to be remnants of a thermalized medium. We analyze the distributions of their multiplicity, charge, and mass, alongside the correlations between these clusters and charged particles. Our findings indicate that the probability of occurrence for heavy-heavy clusters is significantly higher than that for heavy-light clusters. Furthermore, the measured correlations between these clusters and charged particles align with predictions from a thermalized medium model.

This paper introduces a dataset of 1,000 news articles regarding the technological advancements in swarms of military UAVs. We demonstrate that applying Natural Language Processing (NLP) to this collection enables the identification of key topics, the analysis of their temporal evolution, and the extraction of named entities. To achieve these objectives, we employ a combination of unsupervised and supervised NLP techniques.

We introduce a novel method for deriving cosmological parameters by analyzing the three-dimensional correlations of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. This approach relies on the fact that the characteristic scale of the forest's clustering is determined by the sound horizon, a feature imprinted by the acoustic peaks in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest power spectrum. By measuring this scale, we can directly infer the combination of the comoving sound horizon and the Hubble parameter, specifically $r_s/h$. Our technique is applicable to any quasar sample where the mean redshift is sufficiently high, provided the density of quasars allows for the robust measurement of the three-dimensional correlation function. We demonstrate the utility of this method using the SDSS-III BOSS quasar catalog, which contains 10,500 quasias with redshifts exceeding 2.2. Our analysis yields a measurement of $r_s/h = 4.97 \pm 0.41$ (statistical) $\pm 0.21$ (systematic). This result is consistent with the value predicted by the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model.

This paper details the inaugural experimental measurements of both longitudinal and transverse emittance exchange. Utilizing the HIRF test facility at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN), researchers successfully demonstrated the reversal of transverse and longitudinal emittances using a specialized beamline equipped with a cryogenic diamond window. Furthermore, the study confirms the precise control of longitudinal emittance swap by manipulating the longitudinal phase space rotation via radiofrequency (RF) cavities.

This paper introduces a novel sliding-window approach to trajectory forecasting, designed to generate diverse yet socially compliant future paths. The method employs a sliding window to iteratively predict a short time step ahead, allowing the model to capture both immediate and longer-term dynamics. To ensure social compliance, the framework integrates a socially conscious rethinking module that refines predictions to avoid collisions with current agents and static obstacles. Furthermore, the model incorporates a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) to generate diverse outcomes conditioned on the inputs. Extensive experiments across two prominent datasets demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in both diversity metrics and social plausibility.

This study investigates the complexity of Boltzmann machines using two distinct information-theoretic frameworks: variational free energy and network causal complexity. While variational free energy is a standard tool for approximating the partition function and guiding parameter learning, network causal complexity offers a novel approach to quantifying the intrinsic complexity of the posterior distribution. The authors analyze how these metrics behave during learning, demonstrating that variational free energy remains a reliable guide for optimizing parameters, whereas network causal complexity exhibits non-monotonic behavior. Specifically, this complexity initially decreases as the model learns a data distribution, only rising again as it adapts to the true data distribution. The implications of these findings for understanding model learning dynamics are discussed.

The rapid advancement of robotics and artificial intelligence has spurred significant interest in Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI), a field focused on coordinating multiple robots through collective actions. While current HSI research predominantly relies on voice commands, this study introduces a novel approach to distributed HS I centered on sequential hand gesture recognition. We present a new distributed architecture that leverages the computational power of robot edge devices to identify complex hand motions, thereby enabling more natural and intuitive control methods. To validate this framework, we developed a sequential hand gesture recognizer capable of identifying multi-class motions involving two or three fingers. This system was implemented on the edge computing platform of the iCub humanoid robot, which successfully identified the motions with 90% accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrated the practical application of this technology by controlling a swarm of 12 iCub robots to execute a specific task.

This paper introduces a hybrid approach to blood cell categorization that merges CNN and RNN architectures. The proposed system utilizes a CNN to extract features from images and an RNN to process sequential data, with the sequence length determined by the specific task. The study evaluates two distinct RNN variants—GRU and LSTM—across three classification scenarios: single-class identification, binary categorization, and multi-class classification. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms a standalone CNN model in single-class identification, surpassing it by 0.001 in F1-score. Additionally, the approach yields performance improvements of 0.002 and 0.001 in F1-scores for binary and multi-class categorization, respectively, compared to the CNN-only baseline.

We introduce a steering method to construct the ground state of the spinless Hubbard model, a technique that extends variational adiabatic assembly by utilizing a parameterized wave function to guide the system's evolution. This approach allows for the rapid generation of ground states for arbitrary lattice configurations, circumventing the slow timescales typical of adiabatic methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of this counterdiabatic assembly strategy by successfully generating ground states for various lattices, including the Kagome and star-of-David geometries.

This paper introduces a novel tone mapping algorithm that integrates a high-velocity decoloration step with a well-established single-channel operator. The decoloration phase relies on the hue temperature (HT) metric, a novel color space invariant recently defined by the authors. By utilizing a radial HT map, the method accelerates saturation reduction in highly saturated regions through a rapid, data-driven approach. The tuned grayscale values are subsequently restored using a standard monochromatic tone mappers. The algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated by its ability to process a 4K image in under 0.01 seconds on a standard PC.

We introduce the Exponential Taylor Expansion, a novel technique for approximating smooth functions. Unlike traditional approaches, it leverages the fact that $e^x$ serves as a universal building block for all analytic functions, utilizing its property that the $n$-th derivative at any point equals the function value at that point. By employing a weighted combination of these derivatives, the method constructs an approximation that achieves an error bound of $O(h^n)$, where $h$ represents the step size. We demonstrate that this approach offers superior stability compared to classical methods, particularly when dealing with oscillatory functions or those with rapidly varying derivatives. Furthermore, we provide numerical examples illustrating the method's efficiency and accuracy, highlighting its potential for applications in scientific computing and other fields requiring high-precision function approximation.

We establish that a complete, non-compact, and simply connected metric surface featuring a branched metric with non-negative curvature admits a conformal mapping onto the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$. This result generalizes the work of J. Lohöfer and aligns with the findings of A. Huber and J. C. C. Cheeger-Anderson-Kepler respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any complete metric surface which is $\text{CAT}(0)$ and possesses finite total curvature is isometrically conformal to the punctured complex plane $\mathbb{C}^*$. This finding extends the result by Lohöfer.

We introduce a laser-plasma approach to generating intense photon bunches that drive photon-photon interactions. This method involves directing a laser beam through a plasma medium to create a localized region of high-intensity photon bunches capable of inducing nonlinear effects when colliding with external lasers. The technique leverages plasma wave dynamics to concentrate energy into compact photon sources, offering a novel pathway for exploring fundamental photon-photon scattering phenomena under extreme conditions.

We examine the impact of the $m_{12}$ parameter, which breaks the $Z_2$ symmetry in the soft-breaking phase of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM), on the expected signal yields for the $h \to \tau^+\tau^-$ and $h \to \gamma\gamma$ decay channels of the Standard Model-like Higgs boson. This analysis utilizes the latest CMS and ATLAS experimental data from the 13 TeV LHC run, specifically from Run 2. Our findings indicate that the current experimental constraints on $m_{12}$ are consistent with the Standard Model prediction of zero, implying that the $h \to \gamma\gamma$ channel is more sensitive to variations in $m_{12}$ than the $h \to \tau^+\tau^-$ channel.

This paper introduces a transfer mechanism that converts relational data into RDF, specifically handling shape expressions to ensure semantic alignment between the two forms. Convex regression and boundary estimation are vital statistical challenges with diverse real-world applications, ranging from estimating production frontiers and financial efficiency to modeling dose-response curves and image segmentation. This paper introduces pyStoNED, an open-source Python package designed to address these challenges. The library's core functionality includes estimating piecewise linear convex functions using weighted $L_1$ and $L_2$ norms, as well as generating estimates for production and technical efficiency frontiers. By leveraging the CVXPY framework, pyStoNED offers a user-friendly interface that accommodates a wide array of norm options and supports easy extension to additional models. The paper details the underlying methodology, provides a comprehensive user guide, and illustrates the library's capabilities through various examples.

This study investigates the potential for discovering the Higgs boson through the subtle channel of top-antitop-Higgs production at the LHC. We analyze the process $pp \to t \bar t \phi$ in the context of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM), specifically examining the 2HDM Type I scenario. By utilizing a sample of 300 fb$^{-1}$ collected at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, we examine the decay modes where the Higgs transitions into a pair of bottom quarks ($\phi \to b \bar b$) or charged leptons ($\phi \to \ell^+ \ell^-$). Our analysis reveals that the most favorable sensitivity arises in the Type I model with the Higgs decaying to leptons, yielding a 95% confidence level exclusion limit on the parameter $\xi_b^2 \sin^2\beta$ of 0.0016 for a Higgs mass of 125 GeV.

We introduce a straightforward methodology for adapting large-scale language models to specific tasks without the need for task-specific data, task definitions, or human supervision. Our approach involves freezing the model's weights and utilizing an unsupervised contrastive loss to train a classifier on the target data. We demonstrate that this method yields state-of-the-art performance across multiple domains, including classification, clustering, and retrieval. Additionally, we show that the approach remains effective even when the available data is extremely limited, such as with just a few hundred labeled examples.

This paper introduces a dataset for German speech recognition, developed to support the Kaldi and Espeak frameworks. The collection features 1,000 sentences from Wikipedia, totaling 10 hours of audio, with a focus on the standard Central German dialect. The data was gathered using the Amazon Web Services Cloud Voice platform, which utilized the commercial Espeak-18.04 synthetic speech generator. The study outlines the methodology for creating the dataset and the associated annotation, including the derivation of the necessary Kaldi and Espeak configuration files.

This study presents a comprehensive investigation of 30 candidate Be stars within the 30 Doradus region, utilizing multi-epoch optical spectra and photometric data. The analysis reveals that these objects exhibit diverse characteristics, including distinct spectral subtypes, varying degrees of circumstellar disk density, and different evolutionary stages. The findings indicate that Be stars in 30 Doradus are not merely a uniform class but rather a heterogeneous group, likely comprising both classical and classical-like Be stars. Additionally, the study identifies a significant number of stars in a transitional state, suggesting that the accretion-disk formation mechanism is highly dynamic and that the classical Be state represents a relatively short-lived phase. The results further highlight the presence of stars with unusual properties, such as those exhibiting strong emission lines or showing signs of binary interaction, which may offer valuable insights into the complex physics governing Be stars. Overall, the study underscores the need for continued research to fully understand the nature and evolution of these enigmatic objects.

In recent years, the proliferation of diverse text formats has necessitated the development of Inverse Text Standardization (ITS), a process that converts non-standardized variants into canonical forms. Although data-driven models have largely replaced rule-based methods, their efficacy is often hindered by training data containing formatting inconsistencies. This study investigates the impact of data augmentation on these models, demonstrating that applying augmentation during training substantially enhances performance. Furthermore, we present an augmentation strategy that boosts model efficacy without increasing training time. Experiments conducted on the HPL-100 dataset confirm that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art results.

This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn inequality concerning the first eigenvalue of the Hermitian operator under Robin boundary conditions defined on a smooth boundary. In this context, the eigenvalue problem involves an ordinary differential equation on a half-line where the coefficient function is a Hermite polynomial, and the Robin parameter is a real number. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the minimizers of this inequality are precisely the Wulff balls associated with the perimeter functional.

Kernel methods are highly effective for learning graph embeddings, yet they struggle with graphs that lack node features. This study introduces a new approach to address this limitation by extending graph kernels to incorporate node-level information derived from non-exchangeable graphs. We propose the non-exchangeable tangent kernel (NFT-K), which constructs node embeddings by aggregating graph signals across the Laplacian eigenspace. We demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques on various real-world datasets.

We investigate the impact of correlations on non-Hermitian topological point-gap structures within one-dimensional interacting systems. By employing the density matrix renormalization group, we analyze interacting variants of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Chalker-Coddington models. Our findings demonstrate that interactions can diminish the count of point-gap topological classes by half compared to their non-interacting counterparts. Specifically, in the SSH model, we identify a phase where eigenstates are uncorrelated, allowing the point-gap topology to be deduced from the single-particle band structure. Conversely, in the interacting version of the Chalker-Coddington model, we observe that the point-gap topology is entirely eliminated due to the presence of correlations.

This paper examines the incorporation of social speaker characteristics into synthesized speech. We introduce a novel methodology for creating single-speaker multi-accented datasets by manipulating a base dataset with additional acanth sources. Utilizing these datasets, we train a neural network to isolate acanth embeddings from audio signals. These embeddings are then integrated into a speech synthesis system to generate output reflecting varied accents. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully controls accent variation and effectively synthesizes speech from virtual speakers.

This paper introduces new formations of polyphase Golay complementary sets (PGCS) for various window functions, specifically the Hamming, Hanning, and Blackman windows. Additionally, we present a unified framework for generating new 2N-element polyphase Golay complementary sequences (PGCS) derived from existing 2N-element real-valued complementary pairs through specific transformations. Detecting alterations in remote sensing imagery is a critical task, particularly for hyperspectral images (HSI), which offer rich spectral detail but pose significant challenges for traditional alteration detection methods. This study introduces a novel, fully unsupervised deep learning framework for alteration detection in HSIs, leveraging the representational power of deep learning to overcome these hurdles. The proposed method utilizes Feature Combination Deep Convolutional Autoencoders (FCDAE) to extract discriminative features from both reference and test hyperspectral images. These features are then processed by a fully connected deep network to generate an alteration map. The architecture's design allows it to capture both local and global image characteristics, thereby enhancing its representational capability. The approach was evaluated on three benchmark datasets: the Indian Pines, the Salinas Scene, and the Pavia University datasets. Results demonstrate that the unsupervised FCDAE method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving superior accuracy without requiring any labeled training data.

This study investigates the link between residual entropy and viscosity in molecular fluids, utilizing a framework of model potentials that span from hard-core to soft-core interactions. By employing molecular dynamics simulations, we calculated reduced entropy across various temperatures and densities, subsequently correlating these findings with viscosity data obtained from prior simulations. The analysis reveals that the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity is notably more consistent in soft-core systems than in their hard-core counterparts. Furthermore, we examine how this relationship varies with temperature and density, ultimately deriving a predictive equation for reduced viscosity as a function of reduced entropy.

We introduce a new cosmological model characterized by a periodic evolution of the universe, featuring a sequence of cyclic phases. Each cycle begins with a period of contraction, followed by a transition into an expansion phase. This expansion phase is governed by a cosmological constant, allowing the model to be expressed within the framework of $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. We demonstrate that the density of matter and radiation decreases over time, while the cosmological constant remains constant. We also investigate the implications of this model for the cosmic microwave background radiation and the large-scale structure of the universe.

The Invariant-set theory, a superdeterministic model, posits that quantum randomness is an illusion masking a deeper deterministic reality. It asserts that only specific points within a larger phase space are physically significant, and these points form invariant sets that remain unchanged under coordinate transformations. This study introduces a hidden-variable framework to examine the Invariant-set theory's predictions regarding Bell's theorem and quantum entanglement. We demonstrate that Bell's theorem can be resolved by incorporating hidden variables into the Invariant-set model, thereby showing that the Invariant-set theory is compatible with quantum mechanics.

Keyphrase detection, a well-established Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, involves locating significant phrases within a given context. Although deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art results on desktop systems, their heavy computational requirements make them unsuitable for IoT environments where resources are severely limited. This paper introduces a method to adapt DNNs for keyphrase detection specifically on IoT hardware, achieving a 90% reduction in memory usage and a 70% reduction in computation compared to desktop implementations, while maintaining similar accuracy.

The paper examines the correlation functions of 2D fermions situated in a background gauge field, demonstrating that their behavior mirrors that of critical dimer systems. This analysis extends the established duality between the Kasteleyn determinant and the partition function of free fermions to include charged free fermions within such a field. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the computation of the Schwinger function for the vector potential, $V^{\mu}$, and enables the calculation of the vacuum polarization tensor, $\Pi^{\mu\nu}(k)$, for 2D massless fermions.

Group Lasso serves as a widely adopted tool for variable selection in high-dimensional contexts where predictors are organized into predefined groups. While most existing research assumes continuous data, nominal variables are frequently encountered in real-world applications. This study introduces a novel approach for handling high-dimensional nominal variables within a group Lasso framework. We first transform nominal variables into a binary matrix format and subsequently apply a weighted soft-thresholding technique to the resulting columns. This method offers a more flexible and precise strategy for selecting nominal variables compared to current techniques. We further establish theoretical guarantees for variable selection accuracy and demonstrate the method's effectiveness through extensive simulations and real-data analysis.

The hypervisor is a critical component in modern virtualization, yet it is often overlooked in real-time embedded systems, where hypervisor-induced overhead can degrade system performance. This paper introduces T-Visor, a novel hypervisor designed specifically for real-time embedded environments that supports mixed criticality levels. By leveraging hardware virtualization capabilities, T-Visor achieves low latency for high-importance tasks while maintaining a small footprint. Furthermore, the work presents a comprehensive analysis of T-Visor's performance, including its impact on task schedulability.

Panoramic stitching involves merging multiple images captured by a camera to generate a wide-angle view. This process relies on estimating camera poses and aligning feature points across images. While traditional methods often depend on external sensors like GPS and IMU, these devices can be unreliable or unavailable. This paper introduces a novel approach to panoramic stitching that utilizes gravity as a prior to enhance pose estimation. By integrating gravitational information, the proposed method achieves more accurate results with fewer input images than conventional techniques. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing approaches in stitching quality.

This study investigates a system comprising two identical cohorts of phase oscillators, where each group is internally homogeneous yet coupled to the other via heterogeneously distributed interactions. The analysis focuses on the system's dynamical behavior, specifically the conditions enabling chimeras and the mechanisms driving their stability. The findings indicate that a chimeric state emerges when the coupling strength surpasses a critical threshold, a value that is notably lower than the minimum coupling required for chimeras in a three-group configuration with uniform interaction heterogeneity. Furthermore, the stability of the chimera is enhanced by increasing the magnitude of the coupling parameter.

This study addresses the challenge of developing robust controllers for nonlinear systems characterized by both internal and external uncertainties. We introduce a novel data-driven approach that integrates system identification with policy optimization. By leveraging identified models, the method employs a probabilistic framework to synthesize a policy resilient against such uncertainties. The proposed algorithm utilizes a probabilistic model-based search, incorporating a learned transition density to guide the optimization. The paper provides a theoretical analysis of the model's accuracy and the resulting policy's resilience, supported by a numerical case study that demonstrates the approach's effectiveness.

We establish a connection between the higher slice spectra $T_{n,r}$ and multi-layer diagrams, which are specific types of motivic spectra. Our findings demonstrate that multi-layer diagrams account for the entire rational homotopy type of higher slice groups, demonstrating this equivalence at the prime 2 for groups of the form $T_{4,r}$ and at odd primes for groups of the form $T_{2r, r}$.

We investigate the entanglement entropy of the ground state within chaotic matrix product states (MPS) as they evolve under local unitary transformations. Our findings indicate that this entropy is governed by a refracted component, which is determined by the entanglement entropy of the evolving unitary operator itself. This refracted term exhibits a linear increase with the system size, with a slope equivalent to the entanglement entropy per unit length in the initial ground state. Additionally, we demonstrate that the complete entropy asymptotically converges to the total bond dimension of the MPS representation.

Information theory has become a vital tool for analyzing complex systems, with significant research dedicated to quantifying the mutual relationship between input and output. However, most existing studies overlook a critical aspect: the inheritance of information across generations. This paper introduces a framework for analyzing information inheritance within stochastic processes, illustrated through a generational model of a binary variable. We demonstrate that a simple Markov chain can effectively transmit information over many generations, provided the signal-to-noise ratio remains sufficiently high. Furthermore, we explore how non-Markovian dynamics influence this inheritance process.

This work introduces a novel methodology for generating three-dimensional generalizations of the h\'{e}non map, a widely recognized two-dimensional dynamical system. By employing this new technique, we investigate the creation of three-dimensional invariant tori and the divergence of trajectories within hyperbolic sets.

This study examines the concept of holonomy within the framework of loop quantum gravity, demonstrating that it is fundamentally rooted in the non-abelian character of $SO(3,1)$, the Lorentz group governing four-dimensional spacetime. We demonstrate that the unique definition of gravitational holonomy can be constructed exclusively through the adjoint action of the Lorentz group on its Lie algebra, applicable to any spacetime dimension. This formulation applies universally to any curve within spacetime and does not rely on specific coordinate systems. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this definition for the canonical theory of loop gravity.

This work examines the discrete probability distributions governing hook lengths in Young diagrams that are the product of two or three integers. We establish asymptotic approximations for the mean and variance across various cases, with the exception of the scenario involving the square of an integer where the asymptotic mean is resolved but the variance remains open.

We introduce a method to measure the tunneling duration of a single particle using a Larmor clock, where the tunneling time is deduced from the clock's final spin orientation. Because the measurement of this spin angle inherently disturbs the clock's state, it generates a specific type of quantum noise. We demonstrate that this tunneling-induced spin disturbance can be utilized to measure the duration of the tunneling event itself.

We investigate the twist distribution profiles for nonrelativistic P-wave mesons, demonstrating that the profiles for twists 3 and 4 are governed by the same nonperturbative parameters. Consequently, the ratio of these two distributions is determined by a dominant twist 3 contribution, which is largely independent of the meson's quantum numbers. This finding allows us to establish a universal relationship between the $d_{3}^{(4)}$ and $d_{3}^{(3)}$ profiles for P-wave mesons. Using this relationship, we calculate the ratio of twist 4 to twist 3 for the $D_{sJ}^{*}(2732)$ meson, obtaining a value of 0.25.

We investigate a Bose-Einstein condensate within an optical cavity, driven by a two-mode coherent field, and analyze its behavior under various coupling regimes. Our findings reveal that this setup can host multiple quantum switches, characterized by a bistable response to the driving field. We examine the influence of dissipation on the stability of these quantum switches and demonstrate that a Kerr nonlinearity within the cavity can either intensify or diminish the magnitude of the switching effect.

We examine the asymptotic symmetries of four-dimensional massless scalar theories, demonstrating that the BMS algebra emerges in the infrared limit of the corresponding asymptotic algebras. We establish that the leading and subleading soft graviton charges generate the BMS algebra and act on the S-matrix as Kac-Moody generators. Furthermore, we explore the connection between the Kac-Moody representation of these charges and their generator role, while also discussing implications for celestial holography.

This study introduces an innovative neural ensemble architecture designed for continual learning in an online setting. The primary challenge addressed is preventing catastrophic forgetting while maintaining learning efficiency. To achieve this, the model utilizes a dedicated structure that enables the selective activation of specific neurons for learning new tasks without disturbing the parameters established for previous ones. This mechanism facilitates the retention of old knowledge, allowing the system to adapt to new data streams effectively. The work includes a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the model's behavior alongside extensive experiments on continual learning benchmarks. The results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both preserving prior task information and achieving rapid convergence to new tasks.

We define a class of four-dimensional geometric objects known as generalized Shapots, which are constructed by taking the union of four smooth, simple closed surfaces, denoted as $\Sigma_1, \Sigma_2, \Sigma_3$, and $\Sigma_4$. These surfaces are arranged in two concentlic pairs, where $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$ are nested within one another, and $\Sigma_3$ and $\Sigma_4$ form another nested pair. The configuration is such that $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$ are situated inside the volume bounded by $\Sigma_3$ and $\Sigma_4$, respectively. The authors establish that the space of Ricci-flat, asymptotically hyperbolic four-metrics exhibiting these specific topological features is not empty.

This paper investigates permutation functions of the form $x \mapsto (x^q+H(x))^\epsilon$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$, where $q$ is an odd prime power, $H(x) \in \mathbb{F}_{q^3}[x]$ is a polynomial, and $\epsilon$ is an integer. We determine the specific conditions required for a function to be a complete mapping permutation function or a complete permutation function. Additionally, we derive several new complete mapping permutation functions and complete permutation functions using this approach.

This paper introduces a Deep Belief Network (DBN) approach to classify adult *Ascaris lumbricoides* and *Trichuris trichiura* worms based on digital images. These parasites are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in developing nations, necessitating effective treatment. Accurate diagnosis of worm species is crucial for administering the correct antiparasitic therapy, as treatments vary by species. While current diagnosis relies on manual examination of stool samples by medical professionals—a process that is both time-consuming and error-prone—this study presents a novel, automated solution. By leveraging a DBN trained on high-resolution imagery, the proposed method achieves a 98.5% accuracy rate in distinguishing between the two parasite types, offering a significantly more efficient and reliable alternative to traditional manual inspection.

This study examines the optimal reinsurance and investment strategies for two competing insurance firms operating within a jump-diffusion regime-switching framework. By employing the principle of mean-variance optimization, the authors construct two distinct zero-sum games to derive optimal solutions. The analysis proceeds by first establishing the existence and uniqueness of solutions to associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs (HJBI) systems. Subsequently, the optimality of the derived strategies is verified via verification arguments. The final section presents numerical simulations to illustrate the impact of varying jump intensities and regime-switching dynamics on the optimal outcomes.

This paper examines low-energy pion-nucleon interactions, emphasizing their role as a probe into the fundamental characteristics of strong interactions. We analyze how these interactions reflect the chiral symmetry of the theory and its spontaneous breaking, a framework that governs strong forces at low energies. Additionally, we discuss the influence of the nuclear medium on these processes. The text further explores the theoretical and experimental challenges associated with measuring low-energy pion-nucleon scattering and outlines the progress made in advancing these measurements. Finally, we summarize the current state of the field and identify key future research directions.

This paper details the reconstruction of tracks and vertices within the edge region of the Phase-1 upgraded pixel detector at the CMS experiment. Following a 2019 data-taking campaign at the LHC, CMS collected approximately 100 million tracks and vertices using this new system. The study evaluates the performance of the track and vertex reconstruction algorithms, specifically analyzing the region surrounding the detector boundary. The track efficiency in this area is found to be 90% for single muons and 80% for single jets, with a track-finding resolution of 100 microns. The track-misidentification rate is 10% for single muons and 1% for single jets, with a track-finding resolution of 100 microns. We introduce a novel machine learning approach for classifying the morphologies of active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies in the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) survey. By leveraging the HSC Wide Area Survey data, we identify 100,000 sources with redshifts $z<1$ and magnitudes $19<i<24$ using the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam. Our methodology employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on the HSC data to generate classification maps, which are then used to derive galaxy shapes. We validate this technique by comparing our results with classifications from the Galaxy Zoo 3 project, achieving an agreement of approximately 80% for disk galaxies and 60% for non-disk galaxies. Our analysis reveals that the fraction of non-disk galaxies increases with redshift, rising from 0.25 at $z=0.1$ to 0.35 at $z=0.5$. Furthermore, we observe a significant correlation between the ellipticity of non-disk galaxies and redshift, which strengthens at higher redshifts. These findings align with previous studies on the alignment of non-disk galaxies, suggesting that non-disk galaxies in the HSC survey exhibit stronger alignment than those in the Galaxy Zoo 3 sample.

Short-range correlations (SRCs) within nuclei represent a high-momentum component of the nuclear wave function, characterized by intense neutron-proton pairing. This study investigates the phase-space distributions of these SRCs, utilizing a Monte Carlo approach to generate nuclear configurations based on the spectral function framework. We demonstrate that SRCs are predominantly located in momentum space at approximately $k \approx 2$ fm$^{-1}$, with a density profile that closely mirrors the nuclear density. Furthermore, we illustrate that the number of neutron-proton SRC pairs is governed by the nuclear density, while the spatial arrangement of these pairs remains largely independent of nuclear size.

This paper introduces a new framework for handling complex-valued data within deep learning, specifically targeting the challenge of defining function equality. We define complex-valued deep learning as the composition of mappings that operate within complex vector spaces and demonstrate that the standard approach—relying on real-valued norms—is insufficient for rigorous mathematical analysis. To resolve this limitation, we propose a new method for establishing the equality of these mappings. We further show that our proposed definition is consistent with established real-valued norms and provide empirical evidence through experiments on complex-valued classification tasks.

The saturation of parton densities is a fundamental feature of the high-energy regime of QCD, which is essential for explaining the observed behavior in both the low-$x$ region of the deep inelastic scattering process and the large transverse momentum ($p_T$) distribution of hadrons generated in nucleus-nucleus collisions. This review examines the theoretical foundations of saturation, its manifestation in experimental data, and its consequences for the evolution of parton densities. We also explore the concept of geometrical scaling, which characterizes the high-energy behavior of the structure function $F_2$ and the hadronic cross section, and its role in explaining the observed hadronic spectra. Furthermore, the paper discusses the connection between saturation and the formation of the color glass condensate, along with its implications for the initial state of heavy nucleus collisions.

We investigate the elemental abundance spreads within low-metallicity stars to determine if they stem from intrinsic chemical evolution or extrinsic accretion. By analyzing a sample of 100 metal-poor stars from the APOGEE survey, we measured abundances for 12 elements across 10 different bins of metallicity. Our findings indicate that abundance spreads are largely independent of metallicity and element-specific, except for alpha elements, which show a dependence on [Fe/H]. We further examined the correlations between abundance spreads and [alpha/Fe] ratios, finding no significant relationship. These results suggest that intrinsic chemical evolution is the primary driver of these spreads, with extrinsic accretion playing only a minor role.

This study introduces a novel toolkit designed to assess the sensitivity of machine learning forecasts, offering a practical approach to address the critical challenge of model instability in finance. By applying this framework to the problem of predicting financial literacy, we demonstrate its utility. Our analysis reveals that while machine learning models can accurately predict individual financial literacy levels, their performance is highly sensitive to the specific algorithm employed. Furthermore, we observe that the predictive power of individual financial behaviors varies significantly across different machine learning methods.

This paper introduces a learning framework for quantum computing based on the Single Quantum Unit Device (SQUID), a two-qubit system capable of performing basic matrix operations. We demonstrate that a SQUID can execute the core components of a Quantum Neural Network (QNN), specifically a forward pass and a backward pass. During the forward pass, the device prepares a specific two-qubit state representing the input. In the subsequent backward pass, the device applies a Hadamard gate to both qubits, measures the resulting state, and utilizes the measurement outcomes to compute the gradient of a chosen cost function. We also present a method for calculating this gradient without resorting to the traditional finite difference approach. Finally, we discuss the potential for using SQUIDs to train specific quantum gates.

This paper introduces and examines the novel concepts of pointwise semi-slant distorted product submanifolds within the framework of nearly contact metric manifolds. We establish that any such distorted submanifold within a distorted nearly contact metric manifold must be either anti-invariant or invariant. Furthermore, we explore the geometric properties of distorted product pointwise slanted submanifolds, specifically the distorted and semi-slant variants, within a distorted nearly contact metric setting.

The PALEOCCENE project aims to construct a neutrino observatory capable of detecting low-energy signals from reactor neutrinos and potentially solar neutrinos. This initiative utilizes a novel technology based on optical color centers within a diamond crystal, which are interrogated using a specialized laser system. This document outlines the project's current status and presents findings from a materials study designed to assess the feasibility of the proposed detector technology.

This study investigates the dynamics of colloidal particles within active matter suspensions subjected to spatially varying activity gradients. We demonstrate that such gradients drive the emergence of effective forces acting on individual particles, enabling the manipulation of these "dynamical colloids." We establish that these effective forces are governed by the local activity gradient and the anisotropic stress tensor of the surrounding medium. Furthermore, we show that the local diffusivity of a colloidal particle is modulated by ambient activity levels, creating a mechanism where higher activity results in reduced diffusivity. These findings are validated through both Brownian dynamics simulations and analytical calculations.

The paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for low-lying excitations in the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE), grounded in a generalized composite fermion model. This model posits that FQHE low-energy states emerge from the interplay between the magnetorotons and the external magnetic field. We demonstrate that the model's predictions align with the established FQHE phase diagram, while also offering a theoretical basis for the recently observed "missing" FQHE phases. Furthermore, we establish a new set of sum rules for FQHE low-lying excitations, which are validated through numerical calculations based on the proposed model.

Clustering constitutes a fundamental challenge in analyzing networked data, with applications ranging from social sciences to epidemiology. This study addresses clustering in the context of epidemic outbreaks on networks, where clusters represent groups of individuals infected during a specific transmission event. We introduce a geometric approach to define these clusters, which involves partitioning the network into subsets that maximize within-group infection probability while minimizing between-group spread. We demonstrate that this optimization problem is NP-hard and develop a polynomial-time algorithm to approximate the solution. We further establish that the method is computationally efficient and achieves approximation guarantees for specific network types, including regular graphs and those with low treewidth. Finally, we validate the approach using both synthetic data and real-world networks, showing that the resulting clusters align with known outbreak dynamics.

The standard method for creating full-sky CMB maps from observational data involves maximum likelihood estimation, which frequently employs periodic convolution with a pixelization kernel. This approach introduces artificial artifacts known as "X artifacts" at locations where the true sky signal has a value of zero. This study demonstrates that utilizing a pixelization kernel composed of spherical harmonics can effectively eliminate these spurious features.

Communication is a fundamental aspect of human existence, yet it is not innate; it is acquired through experience. In this study, we investigate the process of learning to communicate within a multi-agent framework. We demonstrate that, unlike humans, intelligent agents utilizing reinforcement learning with language directives fail to spontaneously develop the capacity for communication. To address this gap, we introduce a learning phase designed to build referential knowledge, enabling agents to effectively interpret language goals. We also examine the role of this explicit training in acquiring referential skills and the extent to which these skills are retained after the training phase concludes.

Quantum process tomography serves as a fundamental technique for characterizing quantum channels, a capability essential for the development of practical quantum technologies. This work introduces a novel method termed shadow procedure tomography, which characterizes channels using an ensemble of randomly selected unitary operations. This approach is applicable to channels acting on arbitrary input and output Hilbert spaces. By utilizing randomly chosen unitaries, the method can fully reconstruct a channel's behavior, a property demonstrated through the analysis of specific unitary sets, including those from the Clifford group and the Cartan subalgebra. The study establishes that the proposed method is both necessary and sufficient for complete channel characterization. Furthermore, the work derives the exact number of random unitaries required to estimate channel parameters within a specified error margin, providing a closed-form solution for the case of completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) maps with Kraus rank one.

This paper introduces a Keen inequality involving the Cheeger constant for convex domains in the plane, which serves as a two-dimensional analogue to a recent result by B. Kawohl concerning $N$-dimensional convex bodies derived from isoperimetric principles. Additionally, we present several related findings concerning the first Dirichlet eigenvalue and the Perron constant associated with the Laplacian operator within these shapes.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly recognized as a viable solution for delivering goods to remote areas lacking robust infrastructure. This paper introduces a UAV routing optimization framework designed to deliver items to multiple sites within a specified timeframe. The study first outlines the problem's characteristics and mathematical model, then proposes a solution utilizing a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) approach. The model accounts for the payload capacity of the UAV, the weight of the carried goods, and the varying travel speeds of the UAV versus ground transportation between locations. The objective is to minimize the total number of UAV missions required to serve all destinations within the time limit. The model's performance is validated through a case study based on real-world data from a pilot project in the Peruvian Amazon.

We employ the renormalization group method to investigate the stability of multi-particle bound states within a two-layer, mutually charged graphene system. Our analysis reveals that, unlike single or double-body interactions where binding is not stable, three or more interacting particles can form stable bound states. Specifically, the three-body potential exhibits a behavior analogous to the Coulomb force, characterized by a renormalization group fixed point that is both infrared-stable and non-trivial.

We utilized scanning tunneling microscopy and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to investigate the conformational states of Sc2TbN@C80 fullerene on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate across varying temperatures. Our findings indicate that the observed conformations are dictated by the substrate's work function, which exceeds that of the molecule, thereby inducing a net negative charge on the encapsulated Yb atom within the Dy2TbN@C80 framework. This charge distribution generates a substantial dipole moment that competes with the molecule's intrinsic preference for a conformational state that maximizes its own dipole moment. Additionally, we identified a temperature-dependent shift in the NMR chemical shift of the Yb atom, which aligns with the observed changes in conformation.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, encompassing a vast array of devices that communicate via the Internet. These devices are characterized by their low computational power, limited memory, and minimal energy consumption. This paper introduces a survey of various algorithms designed to secure IoT networks, with a specific emphasis on energy usage. It outlines the fundamental principles of IoT security and reviews multiple protocols and algorithms across the domains of key management, authentication, and encryption. Finally, it provides a comparative analysis of these algorithms based on their performance metrics, including energy consumption, memory footprint, and execution speed.

This study introduces a sequential Bayesian trial-formulation approach to optimize the Ramsey sequence, specifically the free precession period ($T_1$) and the $\pi/2$ pulse duration ($T_2$). The optimization framework is designed to maximize the Bayesian information gain regarding the estimation of two coupled parameters, $p_1$ and $p_2$, which represent the mean values of a bivariate Gaussian distribution. The parameters $p_1$ and $p_2$ correspond to the measurement probabilities for outcomes "1" and "0", respectively. The measurement model assumes that, for a fixed trial setting $(T_1, T_2)$), the counts of "1" and "0" follow independent Poisson distributions with means proportional to $p_1$ and $p_2$. The proposed method employs an approximate Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to sample from the posterior distribution of $(p_1, p_2)$ given observed data. The optimal trial configuration is then identified by maximizing the Fisher information contained within this posterior. The study evaluates the method's performance using both simulated data and actual measurements from a trapped ion system.

Network centrality metrics are essential for identifying influential nodes within complex systems, yet they often fail to capture the network's inherent multi-scale geometry. This study introduces Gromov Centrality (GCV), a metric designed to address this limitation by leveraging the triangle inequality surplus to quantify the deviation from ideal geometric relationships. By accounting for the intrinsic curvature of a network, GCV offers a multi-scale perspective on node centrality that traditional metrics overlook. We demonstrate that GCV exhibits a high degree of correlation with established centrarity measures while simultaneously providing a nuanced, multi-dimensional characterization of node importance.

This study introduces a new theory of gravity, which we term the "Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravity" (ASTG). The theory is built upon the premise that the gravitational field possesses only two symmetries: spherical symmetry and azimuthal symmetry. The field equations are derived using the Einstein-Hilbert action, and their solutions are presented in spherical coordinates. The resulting metric is expressed as a combination of two functions, $A(r)$ and $B(r)$, which depend solely on the radial distance. The field equations are solved for a static, spherically symmetric mass distribution, and the resulting metric is compared with the Schwarzschild metric. The comparison reveals that the two metrics are identical in the weak-field limit, but they diverge in the strong-field limit. The paper concludes that the new theory offers a more accurate description of gravity in the strong-field regime than the Schwarzschild metric.

This paper investigates matrix pencils within collections that are rigorably equivalent, a concept introduced by the authors in 2019. We demonstrate that any such collection possessing a non-empty interior is structured as a union of a finite number of convex sets, each having a non-empty interior. We also derive several outcomes regarding the boundary of these collections and provide specific examples of rigorous equivalence sets that are neither closed nor bounded. Furthermore, we establish conditions ensuring that collections of matrix pencils with specific structural properties remain intersection-positive under rigorous equivalence.

This paper presents a geometric formulation of T-duality for twisted tori, extending the framework established in \cite{DSV} for torus bundles over tori. We introduce a specific class of torus bundles over tori, termed *proper torus bundles*, and demonstrate that every such bundle possesses a T-dual. This approach generalizes the findings of \cite{DSV} and provides a geometric characterization of T-dualities on tangent and tangent minus one tangent groups for torus and projective spaces, respectively. Furthermore, we establish a characterization of all T-dual tangent groupoids over a torus, thereby broadening the scope of the framework in \cite{DSV} beyond just torus base spaces.

This paper presents a quasi-polynomial time algorithm that embeds a graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$ and $n$ vertices into a graph with treewidth $O(\log^2 n \log \Delta)$. This result generalizes a quasi-polynomial time algorithm by Dvořák for planar graphs, which achieves a treewidth bound of $O(\log^2 n)$. Additionally, we demonstrate a similar result for graphs excluding a specific class of subgraphs. We prove that for any fixed $k$, a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$ containing no $K_{1,k}$ subgraph can be embedded into a graph with treewidth $O(\log^2 n \log \Delta)$.

This study investigates discrete-time dynamical systems defined by $x_{t+1} = F(x_t)$, where $F$ is a strongly monotone $C^1$-smooth function on a convex domain within a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Strong monotonicity ensures that the system possesses a unique stable fixed point, $x^*$, which acts as a global attractor for all initial conditions. We demonstrate that, under these conditions, the system exhibits a specific widespread behavior: the trajectory of any initial point $x_0$ converges to $x^*$ along a path that visits every open subset of the domain infinitely many times. This result is achieved by establishing a link between the continuous-time dynamics of the system and its discrete-time counterpart, showing that the trajectory of the associated continuous system is $\epsilon$-close to the trajectory of the discrete system for any $\epsilon > 0$.

Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are widely recognized as a primary method for near-term quantum computers to simulate electronic structures. While standard VQE implementations rely on single-qubit gates and pulses, this study introduces a novel variant that incorporates double-qubit excitations. By utilizing a single qubit-driven approach, this new method generates two-qubit entanglement through controlled collisions, allowing for the creation of double-excitation parameterized operators within the ansatz. This results in an adaptive VQE framework that is more qubit-efficient than current alternatives. The proposed protocol was validated by simulating the ground-state energy of the hydrogen molecule ($H_2$) using both classical and quantum-inspired hardware. The simulations demonstrated that the new qubit-excitation-based adaptive VQE achieves comparable accuracy to established methods while utilizing fewer qubits.

The paper introduces a new generative model designed to produce samples that are indistinguishable from those of a given distribution. Unlike many existing approaches that rely on optimizing parameters to approximate a target data distribution, this method utilizes an original, untrained generative architecture. By allowing the generator to learn a representation of the input data through its factor, it generates samples by optimizing these representation parameters for each sample point. Theoretically, this approach is proven to converge to the true data distribution under MAP estimation of the generative model's parameters. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by applying it to both variational autoencoders (VAEs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs). In the case of VAEs, the method eliminates the need for variational inference and KL divergence minimization, thereby recovering the true posterior. For GANs, the method successfully addresses the challenges of non-existent density estimates and unstable training dynamics.

The recent detection of the Hubble tension and the H4 anomaly within the cosmic microwave background (CMB) suggests a potential new physics component in the early universe. We investigate the impact of a gravitational-wave (GW) background generated by a first-order phase transition (FOPT) occurring at temperatures exceeding the electroweak scale. By utilizing constraints from NANOGrav and Advanced LIGO-Virgo, we determine the allowable parameter space for such a background. We further examine how this background influences GW detection rates from binary black hole and binary neutron star mergers, as well as the accuracy of cosmological parameter estimation. Our findings indicate that a GW background from a first-order phase transition at temperatures above the electroweak scale can simultaneously address the H4 anomaly and the Hubble tension.

This study reports the first comprehensive analysis of a comet using the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). We conducted a survey of the coma of C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) at a heliocentric distance of 2.8 AU, utilizing 12 frequency channels to detect emissions from CO, CS, and SO$_2$. Our observations reveal a coma that is spatially extended and non-uniform, with a significant concentration of carbon monosulfide (CS) located approximately 1000 km from the nucleus. This CS distribution suggests a spatially distributed source, potentially arising from the sublimation of CS trapped within the nucleus or the interaction of the nucleus with the interstellar medium. Furthermore, we detected a substantial amount of CO extending up to 10,000 km from the nucleus, a distance far exceeding typical expectations for CO sublimation. This anomaly may indicate a similar distributed source mechanism or the presence of a substantial CO reservoir in the coma.

This paper presents a novel, unsupervised framework for speech generation. By leveraging the contrastive learning paradigm, our method trains a generator and a discriminator in an adversarial setup to maximize the distance between the learned latent codes and their one-hot encodings. This divergence forces the generator to synthesize speech that is more diverse and realistic. The approach requires no annotated transcriptions and relies solely on an unlabelled speech corpus for training. Experimental results on the LibriSpeech test-dev set demonstrate that our system achieves a significantly lower CQR score compared to the baseline, while also producing superior synthesized audio quality.

This study investigates the evolution of the universe within the context of holographic dark energy, specifically focusing on the vitality model proposed by Feng et al. (2010). We analyze the dynamics of this dark vitality using a Tsallis holographic dark energy framework, where the energy density is defined by the relation $\rho_d = \frac{3\omega c^2}{\lambda^2} \left[ 1 - \left( 1 - \frac{\lambda^2}{9\omega c^2} R^{\alpha} \right)^q \right]$. In this formulation, $R$ represents the Ricci scalar, $\omega$ is the Tsallis index, and $q$ serves as the non-extensivity parameter. We further explore the scenario where the Hubble parameter $H$ is treated as a complex quantity, $H = H_1 + iH_2$, with $H_1$ and $H_2$ representing its real and imaginary components respectively. Our results indicate that the equation of state parameter for Tsallis holographic dark vitality is $w_d = -\frac{R}{3\lambda^2} \left[ 1 - \left( 1 - \frac{\lambda^2}{9\omega c^2} R^{\alpha} \right)^q \right] - \frac{1}{3}$. This study introduces a novel algorithm designed to tackle Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) challenges. The proposed method employs a two-stage strategy: initially, it utilizes a Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) to generate a high-quality initial population for the branch-and-bound framework. Subsequently, the branch-and-bound component addresses the sub-problems arising from the relaxation of integer constraints. The algorithm's efficacy is validated through its application to a complex real-world case study involving the design of a multi-stage multi-product chemical plant. Results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms both a standard branch-and-bound implementation and a baseline NSGA-II algorithm.

This work demonstrates that in the setting of Synthetic Differential Geometry (SDG), the integration of group theory with the theory of topological spaces yields SDG's specific framework of topological group theory. Within this context, we establish that linked differential groups—defined as topological groups where the underlying space is linked Lie group—are characterized by being both connected and complete with respect to every possible differential equation.

The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the critical necessity for secure, efficient data exchange within the life sciences. Although various data portals and cyberinfrastructures have been developed to support life science research, they often fail to accommodate the complex, multi-source data exchange scenarios required for large-scale public health challenges. This paper introduces a novel approach to biomedical data exchange that leverages existing data portals and cyberinfrastructures. We present a practical framework featuring a gateway service designed to integrate diverse data sources, alongside a governance model that ensures safe and effective data sharing. This framework was implemented using the Life Sciences Data Exchange (LSDE) LSDF, a new cyberinfrastructure gateway built upon the Data Management Framework (DMF). We demonstrate the system's capabilities by executing a COVID-19 data exchange task, highlighting its potential to address complex, multi-source data integration needs in large-scale research initiatives.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to determine the sentiment polarity toward specific aspects within product reviews. While recent advances have largely focused on sentiment representation, the implicit sentiment toward aspects—sentiment lacking explicit sentiment words—remains underutilized. This study introduces a novel framework called iSPoT, which utilizes supervised contrastive pre-training to identify implicit sentiment. The framework consists of two stages: (1) pre-training a model to predict masked aspects within sentences, and (2) fine-tuning the model for ABSA tasks. During pre-training, the model learns to distinguish between implicit and non-implicit sentiments by contrasting the representations of masked aspects with those of non-aspects. Experimental results on the SemEval-2014 dataset demonstrate that iSPoT achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing previous methods by 1.1% and 1.4% in both binary and three-class sentiment classification tasks, respectively.

This paper examines a causal identification and estimation strategy for indirect effects in the presence of an unobserved confounder, utilizing data from a randomized trial with case-control sampling based on a binary mediator. We establish identification through the use of a weighted full-data model, introducing a weight function that accounts for the probability distribution of the complete dataset. Consequently, we develop and apply an estimation procedure employing weighted full-data inverse probability weighting. This method is demonstrated to be consistent and asymptotically normal under standard regularity conditions. Furthermore, we derive an asymptotic variance estimator for the proposed estimator and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate its finite-sample performance.

This paper investigates transmission phase optimization within Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-aided secure multiuser communication systems affected by hardware impairments. We formulate a non-convex optimization problem aimed at maximizing the minimum secure rates for all users, subject to unit-modulus constraints and realistic linear-per-power amplitude amplitude phase shift errors. To address these challenges, we first relax the unit-modulus constraint and employ the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to derive a suboptimal solution. Subsequently, we refine this result using a projection-based iterative algorithm to satisfy the unit-modulus requirement. Furthermore, we incorporate a low-complexity benchmark scheme based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for comparison. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the benchmark scheme, achieving significant improvements in the minimum secure rate.

This study introduces a new approach to executive reward, termed Executive Ability (EA), which contrasts with traditional methods that rely on handcrafted, static signals. While prior research has largely focused on optimizing these fixed external incentives, our work proposes a dynamic, internal learning mechanism. Specifically, EA utilizes an agent's own past trajectories to generate its own reward signals. By employing a contrastive value estimation strategy, the system identifies and prioritizes high-performing segments of experience for reprocessing, while simultaneously filtering out low-performing data to prevent duplication. Furthermore, the agent's own historical actions serve as a basis for assigning labels during this reprocessing stage. Empirical results across multiple environments demonstrate that EA surpasses both standard internal learning techniques and external, hand-designed reward structures.

While the solar wind is the most studied of these fluctuations, the solar breeze—a low-frequency regime—has received less attention.
