This paper outlines the winning strategy for the NeurIPS 2022 Visual Domain Adaptation challenge, which aimed to generalize models trained on source data to unseen target domains. Our method achieved first place in the unsupervised setting and second in the supervised setting. The core of our approach involves leveraging pre-trained models from the COCO dataset to generate pseudo-labels, utilizing these to fine-tune a domain-invariant backbone, and employing a multi-scale feature fusion technique.

Metric learning methods, such as t-SNE, are widely used to learn representations for high-dimensional data by optimizing distances between data points. However, these methods typically assume Euclidean geometry, which is unsuitable for data residing on spheres, such as vectors with unit norm. This study introduces Spherical Neighboring Embedding (SNE), an adaptation of t-SNE designed for spherical data that utilizes the geodesic metric. We further propose a novel method, VMF-SNE, which integrates variational message passing with geometric deep learning to learn representations for spherical data. This approach is trained by optimizing the proximity of points within the latent space to their respective geodesic distances on the sphere. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We examine the fermi polaron within a two-dimensional electron-impurity model featuring a short-range interaction, employing a Diagrammatic Monte Carlo approach. By computing the polaron's self-energy up to the 10th order in perturbation theory, we determine its ground state energy and effective mass. Our findings indicate that, for weak attractive potentials, the polaron mass exceeds that of the three-dimensional counterpart, whereas in strongly attractive regimes, it is lighter.

This work introduces a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach to emulate fermionic systems, leveraging the advantages of both methodologies. We implement the analog layer using Qubit-Link gates to adiabatically emulate specific fermionic Hamiltonians, while the digital layer applies quantum subroutines to the resulting state to calculate desired observables. To illustrate the method's efficacy, we emulate a one-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model and a two-orbital model featuring spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, we apply digital quantum techniques to determine the ground state energy of the spin-orbit coupled system. These results are validated against classical exact diagonalization and compared with outcomes from recent analog-only digital-free approaches.

We examine a specific type of polynomial sequence derived from undirected graph traits, where traits are defined as minimal induced subgraphs representing equivalence classes of graphs. We establish criteria for determining when such a sequence forms an orthogonal polynomial basis over the space of graphs, with a particular focus on the traits of independent ratio (IR) graph families. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the traits of path graphs constitute an orthogonal basis over all path graphs, provided the weighting function adheres to a particular differential equation.

This paper introduces a novel link invariant defined on the mapping class group's Hitchin component, specifically the "Hitchin link," which functions as a collection of weighted, oriented simple closed curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We establish that this new invariant is sensitive to the braid closure; that is, if the closures of two braids are not distinguished by the invariant, the braids themselves were not distinguished by it. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the invariant detects the braid's braiding number. Finally, we prove that any two links sharing the same invariant are isotopic within the mapping class group's mapping class.

The rise of telecommuting has significantly altered how software is developed, yet its specific impact on the performance of agile projects remains unclear. This study investigates how the proportion of remote workers influences the success of Scrum projects. Using a dataset of 100 completed Scrum projects, we employed linear regression to analyze the relationship between telecommuting levels and project outcomes. Additionally, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 12 Scrum Masters to gain deeper insights into how remote work affects project success. Our findings indicate that while a higher percentage of remote workers negatively correlates with project success, the degree of this impact is moderated by the specific challenges identified by the Scrum Masters during our interviews.

This study reports the measurement of elliptic flow ($v_2$) for beauty-hadron decay products in central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV, utilizing the LHCb detector at the LHC. The analysis covers centralities from 0–60% and examines transverse momentum ranges from 1 to 20 GeV/$c$. Beauty-hadron decays are identified via dimuon channels, specifically $B^{\pm} \to J/\psi \pi^{\mp}$ and $B^{\pm} \to D^{\mp} K^{\pm}$, with the latter serving as the primary source of background. The study finds that the measured $B$-meson decay product elliptic flow is consistent with that of charged pions, indicating that beauty-hadron decay products participate in the collective expansion of the quark-gluon plasma.

The Steadfast Homology theory, introduced by the second author, serves as a combinatorial framework for investigating the stable homotopy groups of chromatic connective theories. In this paper, we demonstrate that the inclusion map from the chromatic connective $E(1)$-based theory into the full connective $E(1)$-based theory induces an isomorphism on steady homology groups. This result extends to the broader family of connective $E(n)$-based theories.

This paper investigates the performance gap between binary power control and optimal continuous power allocation in $K$-user interference channels (ICs) under a fixed sum power constraint. We demonstrate that the optimal GDoF gain offered by optimal power allocation scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This finding is achieved by deriving a lower bound on GDoF for binary power control, which we establish using a specific coding scheme, and by constructing an upper bound that relies on a GDoF-achievable strategy for a related Gaussian interference channel featuring a specific cross-link gain structure.

The primary goal of auditing is to evaluate the effectiveness of an organization's internal controls. While traditional methods rely on sampling to determine control reliability, these approaches are often costly and time-consuming. In contrast, adaptive auditing offers a more efficient alternative by utilizing available data to identify high-risk areas that require further investigation. This paper introduces a novel methodology for adaptive auditing that integrates formal concept analysis (FCA) with the Dempster-Shafer (DS) theory of evidence. FCA is employed to construct a hierarchical concept lattice, which organizes transactions into meaningful clusters. Subsequently, DS theory calculates belief and plausibility measures to assess the significance of these clusters. Consequently, this approach enables the identification of risk areas and the determination of the optimal sample size for further analysis.

This paper presents an innovative algorithm for drawing samples from the Strauss point process, which is a pivotal model in spatial statistics. The proposed method relies on stitching together samples from hard-core point processes. We demonstrate the validity of this approach by establishing a coupling between the Strauss process and the independent set of hard-core processes. The algorithm's performance is evaluated against established methods, including the Gibbs sampler, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, and the rejection sampling technique.

We investigate how the Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) influences the energy spectrum of a charged particle within a constant magnetic field subjected to either Galilean or Lorentz transformations. Initially, we examine the spectrum under a Galilean transformation, deriving the corresponding first-quantized wave equation. Subsequently, we apply the Lorentz transformation to the system, first establishing the second-quantized framework and then calculating the first-quantized Hamiltonian. Finally, we compute the energy spectrum for both scenarios and compare the results.

This study addresses the challenge of scheduling university timetables, specifically focusing on the allocation of shared resources such as projectors and language laboratories. In these contexts, specific courses must occur within facilities equipped for multitasking activities, allowing multiple instances to run concurrently in the same room. The authors introduce a mathematical model designed to minimize both the scheduling duration and the number of required rooms. They propose a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation capable of handling both room-sharing and projectable scenarios, which can be solved using standard optimization solvers. The model's efficacy is validated through computational experiments on a set of real-world university scheduling instances.

This research focuses on modeling, simulating, and analyzing the hopping dynamics of a monopod robot traversing soft ground. Initially, a monopod is treated as a two-degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) inverted pendulum to derive equations of motion using the Lagrangian method. These equations are integrated via numerical simulation to predict monopod behavior on yielding surfaces. Subsequently, a three-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) model is developed to account for yielding terrain effects. In this refined simulation, the ground is represented as a mass-spring-damper system, and the robot's equations of motion are solved using the Runge-Kutta fourth-order method. Finally, the study evaluates the impact of varying parameters on the robot's performance and suggests specific improvements to enhance its behavior on compliant terrain.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with wireless mesh networks serving as a foundational element for many IoT applications. These networks facilitate communication among numerous devices, which can relay messages for one another, thereby extending the network's geographic reach. However, this capability introduces significant reliability challenges, particularly when a device fails to forward messages effectively. To address this, a dependable method for upgrading IoT firmware is essential. This paper evaluates a mesh network comprising 1,000 devices to assess the dependability of firmware upgrades. Our findings indicate that the current upgrade approach suffers from poor dependability, with up to 10% of devices failing to receive updates. Consequently, we introduce a novel, dependable upgrade strategy that successfully reduces un-upgraded devices to less than 1%.

Many-body localization (MBL) represents a rare instance of thermal breakdown in interacting quantum systems. While extensive research has characterized the MBL phase through the lens of many-body Fock space, the transition region beyond localization remains poorly understood. This study investigates the Fock-space propagator within a disordered spin chain to determine the MBL transition point, utilizing a scaling analysis of its eigenfunctions. Our findings reveal that the shift from localized to delocalized behavior coincides with the emergence of multifractality in the spectrum. Furthermore, the shift aligns with the point where multifractality ceases, as evidenced by the vanishing of multifractal exponents.

This study investigates the interactive search problem for multiple targets within a vast search space, where a user seeks to identify the count of existing targets and their specific locations through a limited number of queries. In this framework, a user interacts with an oracle that responds to queries with a numerical count of targets found within the queried subset. We demonstrate that for any target configuration, our proposed algorithm can determine the number of targets and their exact positions with only $O(n \log n)$ queries. Furthermore, we establish that any algorithm requires at least $\Omega(n \log n)$ queries to solve this problem for any target configuration, proving that our algorithm is optimal.

Quantum machine learning (QML) has emerged as a rapidly evolving discipline, with quantum classifiers serving as a foundational component. However, these models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where subtle, imperceptible alterations to input data can force classifiers to produce incorrect predictions. This study introduces a framework for generating adversarial instances and disturbances specifically tailored to quantum classifiers. The proposed method relies on global optimization to identify optimal perturbations that maximize classification error. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated across two distinct platforms: Qiskit, a widely used open-source quantum software library, and PennyLane, a flexible quantum computing framework.

This work examines the Steklov spectrum of a bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^n$ featuring a $C^{2, \alpha}$ boundary, where the shape remains nearly spherical. By employing the Hadamard parametric formula, we derive the first nonzero eigenvalue along with its associated normalized eigenfunction. We further demonstrate that the first eigenvalue is nonzero for any simply connected domain. Additionally, our findings establish the first nonzero eigenvalue for domains exhibiting nearly planar boundaries.

Compliance verification ensures that a system trace adheres to a formal specification. While infix alignment techniques are standard for checking full traces against complete models, they become impractical when comparing trace segments against sub-specifications, primarily because trace segments lack the necessary structure to guarantee soundness in infix analysis. This paper introduces two novel alignment methods—segment-spec alignment and trace-spec alignment—to address this limitation. Segment-spec alignment compares a trace segment against the entire specification, whereas trace-segment alignment performs the reverse comparison. We provide a formal soundness proof for trace-segment alignment and demonstrate its superior efficiency compared to infix alignment through a case study.

Accurate modeling of cellular network signal propagation is essential for optimizing network design and management. While traditional models rely on extensive site-specific measurements, this study introduces a deep learning approach using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to model the path loss between a base station and user equipment. By leveraging the spatial characteristics of geographic data, the proposed CNN architecture generates high-fidelity path loss predictions. Experimental results indicate that the model achieves significant accuracy, surpassing conventional propagation models by 10 dB.

We introduce a standardized, formal definition for planning problems in the temporal domain, addressing a critical gap as temporal domains are a vital yet understudied area of classical planning. This proposal is designed to facilitate the creation of verification tools for planning algorithms, enabling the demonstration that an implementation adheres to these official semantics. We achieve this by employing domain-specific logics to formally define the operational behavior of temporal operators within our semantic framework. Furthermore, we present a sound and complete validation method that utilizes a specialized model-checking algorithm to confirm that a given implementation aligns with these official semantics.

Power system expansion planning (ESP) models are essential for determining the most cost-effective infrastructure investments to meet future demand. These models typically rely on demand forecasts, which are often subject to uncertainty. This study introduces a methodology to quantify the sensitivity of ESP model outcomes to variations in demand uncertainty. The approach utilizes a case study involving a representative ESP model applied to the German power grid, employing a model known as "responsiveness" to measure outcome sensitivity to specific input parameters. The findings indicate that responsiveness is not uniform across all variables; it is particularly high for demand forecasts concerning new generation capacity and transmission line installation, whereas it remains low for existing infrastructure. These insights can assist planners in prioritizing data collection efforts and refining future forecasting accuracy.

This paper examines the global well-posedness of Vlasov-Poisson systems defined within bounded domains. We demonstrate that for any sufficiently smooth initial data, there exists a unique global-in-time weak solution that remains regular up to the boundary. The analysis further establishes that this solution converges to the unique global solution of the standard Vlasov-Poisson system in unbounded space as the artificial boundary is removed. The primary innovation of this work lies in the derivation of precise boundary estimates for the distribution function, which are essential for both proving the existence of these regular weak solutions and establishing their stability under boundary removal.

We introduce a novel approach to identify concepts within a sentence, leveraging a dataset of 1.2 billion queries from a search engine. Our method detects concepts by identifying query matches that share specific lexical items with the target sentence. To enhance the precision of these detections, we employ a position prediction model that refines concept boundaries. Additionally, we have created a new dataset comprising 1.2 million human-annotated concept positions to facilitate training and evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Colloidal gels are highly attractive for numerous applications due to their tunable rheological properties and ability to remain static under flow; however, this very stability often hinders their utility in scenarios requiring active manipulation. This study introduces a novel method to control the viscoelastic behavior and yield stress of colloidal gels using ultrasound. By applying ultrasonic vibrations, the gel's microstructure is temporarily disrupted, causing a shift from solid-like to liquid-like behavior. This transition is characterized by a significant drop in viscosity and a reduced yield stress, allowing the material to yield under minimal stress. This mechanism opens new possibilities for creating "rheo-acoustic" systems where mechanical properties can be actively regulated through acoustic inputs, facilitating the development of advanced applications such as acoustic valves and switches.

Automatically categorizing STEM documents is a critical yet difficult task. While current research predominantly relies on text-based techniques, this study leverages the abundant mathematical content found in such documents to enhance performance. Specifically, we introduce a new entity association approach that constructs a comprehensive knowledge graph by integrating data from multiple STEM sources. This graph enables the creation of specialized representations for both mathematics and general STEM documents, which are then utilized for categorization. Experiments across various domains demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines. Additionally, we present preliminary findings indicating that the proposed representations can also facilitate document classification.

The stable pairings framework allows individuals to submit preference lists without fear of dishonesty, as no one can benefit by altering their reported preferences. A central challenge in this model is determining the length of these lists; if too short, potential matches are missed, but if too long, the risk of including undesirable options rises. This paper introduces a proposal mechanism where agents suggest potential partners to the system, which then decides the final connections. We demonstrate that this method enables individuals to consider only a limited number of proposals while still securing highly preferred outcomes. Furthermore, we outline a specific strategy for proposing partners that guarantees the proposer achieves their top-ranked feasible pairing.

Summary evaluation metrics are essential for assessing summarization models, yet current standards often fail to accurately gauge summary quality. This study introduces SummScore, a new metric that leverages a cross-encoder to deliver a comprehensive and precise evaluation. By training a cross-encoder on a curated dataset of high-quality human summaries, SummScore learns to identify summaries of superior excellence. Experimental results demonstrate that SummScore surpasses existing evaluation standards across multiple datasets and summary types, achieving a significant improvement in alignment with human judgments.

We introduce a new methodology for recovering one-dimensional piecewise smooth functions from noisy data, where the measurements consist of quadratic forms involving the target function and a Gaussian noise vector. This approach is motivated by applications in optical imaging, specifically the reconstruction of images from intensity readings of interference patterns. We establish that a piecewise constant estimator achieves the minimax optimal rate of convergence for both $L_2$ and $L_\infty$ distances, utilizing only a linear number of samples. This result holds even when the noise variance is unbounded, provided the target function is bounded. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to piecewise polynomial functions, demonstrating that the method attains optimal convergence rates in a broad range of smoothness settings.

This paper introduces BEVFusion, a robust and straightforward lidar-camera fusion framework. Unlike many existing methods, BEVFusion employs a simple Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) feature extractor to handle sensor data, eliminating the need for complex projection mechanisms. This design choice streamlines the architecture while delivering superior performance. Furthermore, BEVFusion employs a lightweight fusion module that merges features from both sensors in BEVF space, enabling the model to leverage complementary information effectively. Comprehensive evaluations on the nuScenes and Waymo Open Dataset benchmarks demonstrate that BEFusion surpasses current state-of-the-art fusion techniques, achieving significant improvements in both 3D object detection and multi-object tracking metrics.

The study compares two scenarios: one with adiabatic walls and another with isothermal walls. This study presents a detailed numerical analysis of laser-induced thermal profiles in liquids, aimed at explaining complex diffraction patterns generated by self-induced effects. We investigate the relationship between the spatial thermal distribution and the resulting optical interference fringes, demonstrating that the fringes arise from the interference of laser light scattered by thermally induced density gradients. By modeling the liquid as a dielectric medium with spatially varying refractive index, we calculate the reference wave and the scattered field components. The reference field is approximated as a Gaussian beam, while the scattered field is derived using the first Born approximation. We further employ the Fresnel-Kirchhoff diffraction integral to determine the intensity distribution of the scattered light, which aligns closely with the observed experimental fringes. These findings offer a comprehensive framework for understanding laser-matter interactions in liquids, specifically regarding thermal diffusion and light scattering mechanisms.

This paper introduces a new approach to mining design dialogues, focusing on the conclusion robustness of those designs. We define design dialogues as collaborative discussions where multiple participants work together to create a solution, and we measure conclusion robustness as the degree to which a specific outcome remains consistent despite changes in the input conversation. We present a new dataset comprising 1,000 design dialogues sourced from GitHub, which we utilize to train a model capable of predicting design outcomes and their respective robustness levels. We also evaluate several baseline models and compare their performance against our proposed approach. We believe this dataset and our methods will advance research in collaborative design dialogue analysis and provide valuable resources for future work.

H-STREAM is a novel data stream processing system engineered to handle both current data streams and historical datasets. It is designed to support analytical workflows that combine stream processing with batch operations, enabling the integration of real-time and historical data for downstream analysis. The system's architecture features a distributed, in-memory processing engine capable of handling streaming workloads, alongside a distributed file system optimized for efficient access to massive datasets. H-STREAM facilitates the development of data stream processing pipelines through a high-level DSL, which allows users to define processing logic, processing rates, and the necessary storage infrastructure. The system's capabilities were evaluated by comparing its performance against established stream processing engines and batch processing tools.

We investigate non-resonant graphs for the single production of a top quark and a bottom quark associate, mediated by a charged Higgs boson. This analysis focuses on the non-resonant regime, where the invariant mass of the $tb$ system is significantly lower than the $t+b$ threshold. We examine the contributions of non-resonant graphs to the total cross section for the process $pp \to tbH^\pm \to tb$, specifically for the $tRbL$ configuration. Our findings indicate that non-resonant graphs can alter the total cross section by up to 20% in this scenario. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of non-resonant graphs on differential distributions, observing that they can shift the peak of the $m_{tb}$ spectrum by approximately 10 GeV.

Knowledge-based neural machine translation (KB-NMT) integrates a knowledge base (KB) into a machine translation (MT) system to enhance the generation of sentences lacking sufficient training data. While existing approaches primarily focus on translating knowledge within a sentence, this paper introduces a new mechanism to handle knowledge that spans multiple sentences. We propose a duplicate mechanism that identifies and duplicates relevant knowledge components from the source to the target side of a sentence pair. This approach allows the model to access such information during translation. We evaluate the mechanism using a model based on SPARQL, a query language for RDF knowledge graphs, and demonstrate through experiments that it significantly improves translation quality.

Academic researchers are increasingly aware of the growing influence of venue selection on a paper's impact. While the prestige of a publication venue is often inferred from the citations received by its prior works, this approach is frequently problematic because it conflates venue quality with the broader influence of a research group. To address this, we introduce Venue Insights, a straightforward metric designed to isolate venue quality independent of external citation trends. Our analysis indicates that Venue Insights exhibits a stronger correlation with a paper's subsequent success than traditional venue-level metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this indicator can effectively identify high-quality venues across diverse domains, including Computer Science, Medicine, and Physics.

This paper examines the use of neural networks in control systems, specifically addressing the challenges of training and validating them. It begins by outlining a control framework where a system evolves over a finite time horizon under a chosen policy, with the objective of minimizing a cost function. The problem is then framed as a minimization task for this cost, subject to system dynamics and constraints, which is solved using a neural network as the policy. A key challenge arises because the cost function is difficult to compute exactly due to the need to simulate the system's evolution. Consequently, the work explores the implications of approximating this cost during the training phase and the use of imperfect models for validation. It demonstrates that relying on inaccurate models for validation can lead to policies that appear optimal during testing but result in catastrophic failures when deployed on the actual system.

This paper introduces a novel method for performing overlapping hierarchical grouping in a fully functorial manner. Our approach centers on a new concept: the functorial hierarchy, which is defined as a functor from a finite category to the category of finite sets. We provide a constructive proof demonstrating that every such functor can be decomposed into a composition of specific functorial types known as "elementary functors." These elementary functors are characterized by their behavior on a chosen element within the domain, effectively mapping it to an element in the codomain. We establish that an elementary functor corresponds to a function that is both surjective and partial. Furthermore, we show that this functorial framework extends to the realm of group theory, enabling a functorial formulation of overlapping groupings through the lens of group theory.

Restoring visual data from streaming tensor inputs is essential for numerous real-world applications, including medical imaging, satellite photography, and remote sensing. However, current methods often fail to meet the strict latency and memory constraints required by these scenarios. This paper introduces a new approach for streaming tensor recovery that leverages patch monitoring and tensor ring completion. By utilizing a streaming algorithm to track the trace norm of a low-rank matrix, we can effectively approximate this non-convex measure, which serves as a superior proxy for tensor ring completion. Our method also incorporates an adaptive strategy to dynamically adjust the number of latent factors, balancing reconstruction quality against computational cost. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed technique surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both performance and efficiency.

This paper investigates the structure of the associated graded algebra $\operatorname{gr}\mathcal{B}$ for certain Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}$ derived from $1$-dimensional Yetter-Drinfeld modules over Weyl groups $W$ of types $B_2$, $C_2$, and $D_3$. Specifically, we demonstrate that $\operatorname{gr}\mathcal{B}$ is isomorphic to a quadratic Artin-Schelter regular algebra of dimension 4, denoted as $\mathcal{R}(4,4)$, or to a quadratic Artin-Schelter regular algebra of dimension 5, denoted as $\mathcal{R}(5,3)$, both defined over a field of characteristic 0.

This study provides the first direct numerical confirmation of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) spectrum for inertial wave turbulence. We demonstrate that the energy spectrum follows the $k^{-2}$ scaling predicted by the ZK theory, a result derived from direct simulations of the Navier-Stokes equations within a periodically bounded three-dimensional domain. These simulations were conducted under conditions of strong anisotropy and rotation, utilizing rotation rates significantly exceeding the inertial frequency.

This paper addresses the problem of iteratively standardizing graphs, a problem proven to be NP-hard. We establish that the maximum-weight autonomous subgraphs of graphs with maximum degree 2 are NP-hard to compute, thereby extending the known hardness results for graphs with maximum degree 3. Additionally, we demonstrate that the problem remains NP-hard even when edge weights are restricted to the values 1 and 2.

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of electrically regulated monolayer graphene, utilizing the non-relativistic density functional framework of the Wexler and Keldysh model. This approach allows us to examine the universal characteristics of graphene's electronic system, specifically focusing on the influence of an electric field on its energy spectrum. Our analysis covers the entire range of electric field intensities, spanning from weak to strong regimes.

The binary system CR Draconis, consisting of the flare star CR Aur and its companion, has been monitored using low-frequency radio telescopes (operating between 10 and 30 MHz) to detect electron-cyclotron maser emissions. This study presents the results of a long-term campaign spanning 12 years, which identified radiation from the star at cyclotron frequencies corresponding to magnetic field strengths of approximately 100 Gauss. The analysis reveals that the star's activity is characterized by a power-law distribution of flare energies with an index of $\alpha = 2.1 \pm 0.1$. Furthermore, the frequency of flares exhibiting energies exceeding $10^{30}$ ergs is estimated at roughly 100 events per year.

Artificial intelligence has recently advanced significantly, particularly in the domain of human motion capture. This paper introduces Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), a neural rendering framework designed to generate high-quality, photo-realistic images of articulated human figures from novel viewpoints. Unlike traditional methods, ANR utilizes a single, unified implicit representation capable of modeling both the human body and their clothing. By integrating skeletal kinematics, the system renders realistic imagery based on a skeleton's pose and produces smooth, consistent results across poses. The approach was evaluated on the newly created ARCH dataset, which features high-resolution scans of individuals wearing various garments in diverse poses. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that ANR surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both quality and fidelity for rendering clothed humans.

The proliferation of image manipulation tools has prompted a need to evaluate how these alterations affect human and machine perception. This study investigates the influence of intense image processing on the ability of both humans and machines to detect object categories. Through experiments involving humans and a state-of-the-art machine learning model, we assessed classification accuracy across various alteration intensities. Our results indicate that while humans struggle with classification as alteration intensity increases, machine performance remains largely unaffected. Additionally, we observed that humans tend to rely on global image features for classification under alteration, whereas the machine leverages local features. These findings suggest that image manipulation strategies designed to deceive machines may inadvertently make classification tasks even more difficult for human observers.

We investigate the connection between the 3d Chern-Simons path integral and the 2d TQFT of the spin Teichmuller category. Our primary focus is on the TQFT values of the Hopf link, which we define as "link symbols." We demonstrate that these link symbols are eigenvalues of the Hopf link's matrix representation within the Hopf link's Hilbert space. Additionally, we establish that the algebraic structure of the TQFT, specifically the fusion rules of the spin Teichmuller category, corresponds to the multiplication rules of the link symbols. Finally, we show that the link symbols are polynomials in the variable $k$ (the Chern-Simons level) with coefficients from the complex numbers, and we provide an explicit formula for the TQFT values of the Hopf link's mapping class group action.

We examine the thermodynamic characteristics of 2D frustrated antiferromagnets composed of weakly-coupled equilateral triangles. Our findings indicate that the system undergoes a phase transition to a 120-degree ordered state at a critical temperature $T_c$. By employing the ratio method within the cluster quantum Monte Carlo framework, we determine $T_c$ across various coupling ratios and triangle sizes. Additionally, we analyze the specific heat and magnetic susceptibility near $T_c$ to evaluate the validity of the 2D Ising universality class for describing this transition.

Although large pre-trained language models have proven effective for various natural language processing tasks, they are not inherently suited for zero-shot classification. This paper introduces a method to adapt these models for zero-shot classification by fine-tuning them on a curated collection of classification datasets. We evaluate two distinct fine-tuning strategies: (1) applying prompt-based zero-shot techniques using in-context examples, and (2) adapting the model for direct classification without auxiliary cues. We also present DANCE, a new framework designed to automatically select the most suitable dataset for a given target task. Furthermore, we explore a meta-learning approach to enhance the model's ability to generalize to unseen tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed techniques significantly outperform existing zero-shot baselines.

We examine the impact of finite temperature effects on the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) within the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM), specifically within a $Z_3$-invariant framework. Our analysis indicates that the thermal corrections significantly influence the order of the transition, potentially shifting it from a smooth crossover to a robust first-order event. This shift is primarily driven by the substantial contribution of the light CP-odd scalar, which acts as a key order parameter. Additionally, the presence of light pseudoscalars and charged scalars can markedly alter the transition's characteristics, potentially enhancing its strength and sharpness. These findings have profound implications for both LHC phenomenology and the identification of dark matter candidates. Finally, we explore the potential for detecting gravitational waves generated by this cosmological first-order phase transition, highlighting the feasibility of probing such a scenario with current and future observatories.

We introduce a new tool designed to detect spurious redshifts in high-redshift galaxies, a critical capability for the next generation of cosmological surveys. By analyzing the redshift distribution of 1,000 low-resolution images from the COSMOS field, we find that our method successfully filters out 99.9% of spurious redshifts while retaining 99.9% of genuine ones. This approach is particularly effective at eliminating false detections caused by bright foreground stars, faint background sources, and artifacts from image processing. We anticipate that our technique will become a standard component of future redshift selection pipelines.

We investigate the low-energy dynamical properties of the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice using large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations. By employing a novel analysis technique, we identify the characteristic signatures of the conventional Néel phase alongside those of recently theorized "liquid" phases. Our findings reveal that the nature of the low-energy spectrum is highly dependent on the specific magnetic field orientation. Specifically, when the field is applied within the $ab$-plane, the system transitions from a gapped state to a gapless state at a critical field of $B_c \approx 0.14J$. In contrast, when the field is oriented along the $c$-axis, the gap closes at a higher field, $B_c \approx 0.20J$. These results align with the existence of a symmetry-disrupted liquid phase. Furthermore, our data indicate that the conventional Néel phase persists up to fields of $B \approx 0.25J$ for both field directions.

We investigate the $SU(3)-$Higgs theory on a $3$-dimensional cubic lattice, demonstrating that it possesses two distinct phases: a confining (deconfinement) phase and a deconfinement (deconfinement) phase. In the deconfinement phase, the theory exhibits chiral symmetry breaking, whereas this symmetry remains restored in the confining phase. Furthermore, we identify a first-order phase transition separating these two regimes.

The magnetic structure of the high-temperature antiferromagnet Cr$_2$Al was investigated using neutron powder diffraction, revealing an in-plane hexagonal antiferromagnetic arrangement with a propagation vector of **k** = [0 0 1]. Analysis of the exchange interactions indicates that nearest-neighbor coupling is weakly antiferromagnetic, whereas interactions with second-, third-, and fourth-nearest neighbors are strongly antiferromagnetic.

This study examines a kinetic model featuring a velocity-dependent collision frequency, which is employed to simulate rarefied gas flows characterized by intermolecular potentials that deviate from the standard inverse-power law. The model's validity is assessed through comparisons with the full Boltzmann equation across a range of potentials, including the hard-sphere, Spline, and inverse-power-law forms. The analysis reveals that the model accurately captures the non-equilibrium characteristics of these flows, specifically the non-monotonic variation in bulk viscosity with respect to the potential exponent, as well as the corresponding distribution function and transport properties.

We introduce a novel approach to semantic labeling that leverages extensive pre-training on extensive, unlabeled datasets. Our model learns a high-level representation of the input space, which is subsequently adapted to perform specific tasks using only a small set of labeled examples. We demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in scenarios with extremely scarce data. Our findings indicate that the model's effectiveness is highly sensitive to the choice of pre-training objective. We evaluate several alternatives and identify the Cross-Encoder as the most effective option. Additionally, we observe that incorporating task-specific information into the pre-training phase yields further performance gains.

The future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will investigate the internal structure of protons and nuclei by scattering them against highly collimated electron beams. To precisely determine the three-dimensional positions of scattered particles, the EIC demands advanced silicon tracking sensors that deliver exceptional spatial resolution, high radiation hardness, and the ability to function at low temperatures. This paper reviews the EIC's detector requirements and outlines recent silicon sensor technologies developed to meet them.

This study examines the variability of the low-mass active galactic nucleus (AGN) PGC 1149035, which has a mass of approximately $10^6$ solar masses. We analyzed 11 years of optical photometric data collected by the ZTF survey and discovered that the object exhibits both long-term outbursts and short-term fluctuations. The short-term variations display a quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) with a period of roughly 1.5 days, while the long-term behavior is characterized by flaring events lasting about 100 days. The fluctuations in magnitude are substantial, reaching up to 0.5 magnitudes. We propose that the observed QPO arises from oscillations within the accretion disc, while the flaring events result from instabilities in the outer regions of the disc. This work represents the first identification of QPO in an AGN with a mass below $10^6$ solar masses.

We have conducted a series of high-resolution spectropolarimetric observations of HD58260, a rapidly rotating B2V star, using the ESPaDOnS instrument at the CFHT. The study focused on the Fe ii line at 561.9 nm, which is highly sensitive to the star's radial magnetic field gradient. Analysis of the polarization signals in this line reveals a strong correlation with the star's rotational phase, indicating that the observed effect is primarily rotational rather than spot-induced. The derived magnetic field gradient is approximately 1.5 G per degree, a value consistent with results from previous studies. Furthermore, the observed gradient aligns with the star's rotation period and the rotationally modulated magnetic field, supporting the hypothesis that the star's magnetic field is generated by a dynamo operating in its outer envelope.

We present a bosonic representation of the one-dimensional Gauss hypergeometric Dunkl kernel, expressed using creation and annihilation operators within the Fock space framework. This approach extends the classical boson representation of the singular isompythetor for the Gauss hypergeometric differential equation to include the Dunkl setting. Additionally, we establish a connection between the singular isompythetor and the singular Dunkl intertwining operator, thereby establishing a singular link between the standard boson representation of the hypergeometric differential equation and the singular Dunkl equation.

We present new ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in the starburst galaxy NGC 5253, a region characterized by low metallicity. This study aims to evaluate the H30$\alpha$ emission as a potential tracer for massive star formation in starburst environments. The data reveal a compact source with a full width at half maximum of 10.6 km s$^{-1}$, which is spatially consistent with the galaxy's star-forming core. By comparing the H30$\alpha$ flux with that of the H$\beta$ line, we derive a correction factor of 1.01 $\pm$ 0.15 for the ratio R$_{H30\alpha}$(Z) = L$_{H30\alpha}$ / L$_{H\beta}$, indicating that the H30$\alpha$ emission remains a reliable indicator of massive star formation even under low-metallicity conditions. Furthermore, we estimate the star formation rate within NGC 5253 to be 0.013 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, a value that aligns with results from other tracers.

Continuous orbit similarity rigidity refers to the property where a topological conjugacy that preserves the metric up to a constant factor is actually a similarity transformation. This paper establishes that certain minimal actions of infinite-dimensional Lie groups on spaces are characterized by this property. Specifically, we prove that for an infinite-dimensional Lie group $G$ acting minimally on a compact $G$-space $X$, if the action is virtually periodic, then every homeomorphism $h: X \to X$ that induces a similarity is a global similarity transformation. This result holds for actions of unitary groups on compact metric spaces.

This paper examines the asymptotic properties of Nadaraya-Watson estimators for conditional means, defined by $E[Y|X=x]$. We demonstrate that when $Y$ is a scalar and $X$ is multivariate, the estimator's distributional limit is a location-scale mixture of normals. Furthermore, we establish that the estimator's bias is $o(n^{-1})$ under the assumption that the conditional mean function is sufficiently smooth. These findings extend to cases where $X$ is univariate and $Y$ is multivariate, with a bias expansion of order $o(n^{-1})$ for smooth enough functions. We also analyze estimation bias for $P(A|X=x)$, where $P$ is a conditional probability function, and establish a result regarding the asymptotic normality of the estimator. These findings are applied to construct confidence bands for conditional expectation functions.

This study introduces a novel observer-based approach to estimate the state of epidemics. The authors propose a new framework designed to identify the parameters of a specific compartmental epidemic model, which is subsequently utilized to construct an asymptotic observer. The convergence of this observer is demonstrated through Lyapunov analysis, and the proposed method is validated via simulations on an SEIR model.

Knowledge Graph Forecasting (KGF) involves predicting future entity relations within a knowledge graph. While recent studies have primarily focused on temporal frameworks to handle dynamic graphs, this paper investigates the effectiveness of static models on such graphs. Our findings indicate that static approaches can achieve performance comparable to, or even superior to, state-of-the-art temporal methods. Additionally, we introduce a new static framework that surpasses existing state-of-the-art results. Our analysis reveals that the primary determinant of a model's success is its ability to effectively represent entities and relations, rather than the specific choice between temporal and static architectures.

Ultrashort optical oscillators are vital for advancing numerous scientific and technological areas. This study presents a geometric examination of Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLML) to analyze the beam quality of oscillators operating at peak powers exceeding 10 GW. We demonstrate that the beam quality is contingent upon the ratio of the cavity's thermal lensing to its focusing power. This finding is validated by experimental data from oscillators operating at 80 MHz, achieving peak powers between 10 and 20 GW, and producing beam profiles that align with our theoretical predictions.

This paper introduces an asynchronous online federated learning (FOL) framework designed for nonlinear regression tasks involving time-evolving data streams. In this model, multiple learners with varying computational capabilities and memory constraints collaboratively train a global model by processing data locally and periodically transmitting their updates to a central server. To address the heterogeneity of these learners, we develop a novel algorithm that enables asynchronous learning, allowing each participant to send model parameters based on their specific computational speed and memory availability. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for this approach and demonstrate its superior performance compared to synchronous methods and other asynchronous algorithms. Additionally, we validate the algorithm's effectiveness through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets.

This study introduces a novel silicon membrane architecture designed to enhance light absorption in thin and ultrathin layers by substituting a conventional silicon rear reflector with a photonic crystal structure. The resulting device features a silicon membrane suspended atop a photonic crystal stack built within a silicon dioxide substrate. Utilizing finite-difference time-domain simulations, we demonstrate that this configuration achieves superior absorption compared to traditional designs relying on silicon rear reflectors.

This paper introduces a formula for the complex tetration function, which serves as an extension of the real tetration function introduced by Knesch. The authors propose two primary theorems: the first establishes the formula's uniqueness, while the second provides an asymptotic approximation. The second theorem is derived as a direct consequence of a more fundamental theorem, which establishes the formula's continuity. The authors also present this intermediate theorem in its full generality, applicable to other functions defined by real recursion relations.

We introduce a new family of explicit high-dimensional expanders (HDXs) constructed via group actions on finite sets. These HDXs are defined as the simplicial complexes comprising the orbits of points within the configuration space of $d$ distinct elements from a finite group, where $d$ is a specified dimension. Our construction yields the first known examples of HDXs that are both explicit and satisfy the following properties: they achieve an explicit spectral gap independent of dimension $d$, possess an explicit isomorphism to a regular graph, and maintain an explicit bound on their girth. Notably, our construction yields an infinite sequence of such complexes for any fixed group, with dimensions growing arbitrarily large. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these complexes are not only HDXs but also satisfy the Strong Frankel-Wieland property, allowing us to apply our main result to recover and extend recent findings by Bamberger, Cohen, and Shalev regarding the spectral gap of random Cayley complexes.

This study examines the magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$ through magnetization and specific heat measurements across a broad temperature range and various magnetic fields. The data indicate a quasi-two-dimensional honeycomb lattice structure, with the easy magnetic axis oriented perpendicular to the honeycomb planes. Analysis of the specific heat and magnetization data, utilizing the spin-1/2 Heisenberg model, yields exchange coupling constants of $J_{\perp} = 1.0$ K and $J_{\parallel} = 0.1$ K. Furthermore, the material exhibits a field-induced phase transition at a critical field of $H_c = 1.2$ T, which is confirmed by the presence of a sharp peak in specific heat and a distinct kink in magnetization at this threshold.

Link prediction is a critical task in network analysis, with a primary objective of forecasting future connections. While prior research has largely concentrated on predicting the existence of current links, this study addresses Link Forecasting (LF)—the challenge of identifying edges that will emerge in the near future. We introduce a novel framework that integrates a Sparse Structural Neural Embedding (SNE) model with a Temporal Graph Neural Network (TGNN). The SNE model generates node representations by leveraging both the network's topology and degree sparsity, while the TGNN utilizes these representations alongside historical link patterns to predict upcoming edges. Empirical evaluations on four real-world datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We describe the fabrication and testing of two silicon-based atomic vapor cells featuring etched windows, created using deep silicon etching and glass frit bonding. The first device is a 10 cm³ chamber with a 1 cm² view port, while the second is a 1 cm³ chamber with a 0.25 cm² view port. Both units were evaluated for their light transmission characteristics, window stress, and leak rates. The 10 cm³ model achieved a window transmission of 90% at 780 nm and a leak rate of 10⁻⁹ mbar·s⁻¹. The 1 cm³ model demonstrated a window transmission of 99% at 780 nm and a leak rate of 10⁻¹⁰ mbar·s⁻¹. These results indicate that the proposed design is well-suited for creating compact atomic vapor chambers for applications in atomic clocks and sensors.

This paper introduces a modeling approach for estimating the nonlinear disturbance power of nonlinear systems, specifically focusing on dual-polarization 4D modulation formats. The model is designed to handle arbitrary input signal characteristics, including amplitude distributions, temporal dynamics, and the cross-polarization modulation (XPM) interaction between signals. The proposed methodology was validated using simulations of dual-polarization 4D QAM systems, demonstrating that the predicted nonlinear impairment aligns closely with simulated results.

This paper introduces FIRe-GAN, a novel deep learning-based fusion framework for generating synthetic infrared-to-visible imagery for wildfires. The study addresses the scarcity of training data for such synthetic generation and the difficulty of aligning corresponding regions between modalities. To overcome these obstacles, the proposed method employs a lightweight, unpaired fusion architecture capable of learning robust feature representations. The resulting synthetic images are validated using a state-of-the-art object detection model, which demonstrates that the generated outputs achieve superior accuracy compared to existing methods.

Social media has become a primary source of information for individuals to connect with others, yet it also serves as a platform for sharing personal thoughts and feelings. This study presents a novel method for identifying indicators of depression by analyzing user data. We collected a dataset comprising 1,000 English-language social media posts from individuals diagnosed with depression and a control set of 1,000 posts from non-depressed individuals. This collection was achieved by accessing the Twitter API to retrieve tweets from specific accounts. We conducted an empirical analysis to determine the effectiveness of various machine learning models in distinguishing between depressive and non-depressive content. Our findings indicate that a Random Forest model utilizing word embeddings achieved the highest accuracy of 76.1%, outperforming a Support Vector Machine (SVM) model that relied on Bag-of-Words features, which recorded an accuracy of 68.1%.

This study introduces a stochastic compartmental model for COVID-19 that accounts for the variability in individual infection durations. The population is categorized into four groups: susceptible ($S$), infected ($I$), recovered ($R$), and those who have died ($D$). The model's primary objective is to forecast the epidemic's trajectory and determine the final count of fatalities. The analysis relies on a Markov chain framework, where the transition from the infected state to either recovery or death is governed by a general distribution. The paper begins by defining the associated Markov chain and its transition matrix, followed by an examination of its key characteristics. The authors derive a specific condition for the model's extinction and provide a closed-form solution for the probability of death. The findings are illustrated using real-world COVID-19 data from Italy.

This study investigates the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si using inelastic scattering of $^{12}$C ions, a process that induces significant isoscalar monopole (ISGMR) and quadrupole (ISGQR) excitations. The experimental findings are contrasted with results from the Gogny D1S Skyrme-HFB+RPA theoretical model. The analysis reveals that ISGMR strength is notably fragmented in both nuclei, with a pronounced correlation between the ISGQR and ISGMR components. The study concludes that the observed ISGMR strength distribution is governed by the coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole excitations.

This study examines the long-term behavior of a dynamic system governed by stick-slip motion, driven by elastic forces, Coulomb friction, and a feedback control mechanism. The analysis demonstrates that the system's trajectory converges to a steady state characterized by periodic slip phases alternating with stick phases. This result is established by proving that the system's Poincaré map possesses a unique fixed point, which is both globally stable and approached with exponential speed. Furthermore, the findings are applicable to a broader class of nonlinear control frameworks, including those involving variable stiffness and friction models that deviate from standard Coulomb formulations.

This work addresses the challenge of learning to hedge against model misspecification in environments where the underlying dynamics are unknown. We introduce a novel hedging strategy that is robust to such misspecification, grounded in Bellman hedging—a reinforcement learning technique that incorporates a penalty for the squared deviation of the hedging portfolio from a non-hedging baseline. Unlike previous approaches that rely on a fixed penalty parameter, our method automatically tunes this parameter to ensure convergence to the optimal hedging policy, even when the model is imperfect. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm remains effective in both model-free and model-based settings, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical validation through experiments.

Although sequential recommendation systems are widely used, their ability to uncover the underlying reasons for a user's motivation remains limited. This paper introduces a new model designed to explicitly capture these motivations by leveraging a multi-task learning framework. This approach jointly optimizes a standard sequential recommendation task alongside a motivation prediction task. By utilizing a factorization network to represent the correlation between user motivations and item features, the model effectively links these domains. Consequently, this not only enhances the accuracy of item suggestions but also simultaneously generates reliable motivation recommendations. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that the model significantly improves both recommendation performance and the accuracy of motivation prediction compared to baseline methods.

This work examines a general symmetric unfolding of the source within the double confluent Heun equation (DCHE), demonstrating that it admits transformable double confluent Heun equation (tDCHE) forms. These tDCHE forms are characterized by two specific monodromy conditions: the requirement that the fundamental memory matrix be diagonal and the vanishing of the coefficient for the $y^{-1}$ term in the formal power series expansion of the first fundamental solution. Furthermore, utilizing the established connection between tDCHE solutions and those of the ordinary differential equation (ODE) associated with the Picard-Fuchs equation of a specific family of Calabi-Yau threefolds, the authors derive the corresponding general symmetric unfolding of the source within the context of Calabi-Yau threefolds.

We introduce a novel problem of approximating a rank-one matrix characterized by group-wise heterogeneity, where data is partitioned into groups, each sharing a common angle with the target matrix. This angle serves as the group's heterogeneity level. The study establishes theoretical lower bounds for the minimax risk of estimation regarding both the angle and the angle's rate of convergence. The analysis indicates that the optimal estimation risk scales linearly with the number of groups and exhibits a polynomial dependence on group sizes. Furthermore, we develop an estimator that achieves optimal rates up to logarithmic factors. The theoretical findings are validated through numerical experiments.

The study of topological materials has been significantly advanced by symmetry principles, particularly those governing band structures and symmetry-protected surface states. However, recent research has uncovered topological phases that defy symmetry protection, prompting inquiries into the role of topology in systems devoid of such symmetries. This work introduces a model featuring a non-trivial bulk topology in the absence of symmetry, utilizing a two-dimensional Dirac-like framework with a position-dependent mass. This mass term, which breaks both time-reversal and particle-hole symmetries, generates a non-trivial bulk topological invariant, yielding a series of helical edge states. Furthermore, we examine the stability of these edge states against disorder and perturbations, demonstrating that they remain intact. Additionally, we provide an analytical derivation of the edge state dispersion relation and validate our findings through numerical simulations.

We investigate the LFEE ratio $R_\tau$ within $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions, defined as the cross-section ratio involving $\tau$ leptons to that involving electrons. This analysis examines the $b\to s\tau^+\tau^-$ channel within the Standard Model, utilizing the OPE framework to determine the hadronic matrix element for the scalar and pseudoscalar operators. We find that LFEE is violated in the $b\to s\tau^+\tau^-$ process due to the distinct masses of the leptons, which impact the scalar and pseudoscalar contributions. We also discuss how this violation can be exploited to probe new physics.

This work introduces a distributed control method for linear multi-channel systems that maintains a fully decentralized design while enabling seamless integration of new components. The proposed approach utilizes a network of compensators, each operating with only local data and communicating via a network to achieve stability and performance objectives. By employing a multi-channel framework, the architecture ensures a completely distributed structure where the regulation task is addressed through a specific design of distributed dynamic gains. The method is demonstrated to possess an inherent plug-and-play capability, allowing for the reliable addition of compensators without disrupting the stability of the overall system.

The ongoing global pandemic has caused significant disruption to daily life, resulting in thousands of fatalities and billions of dollars in losses. To mitigate the impact, governments have implemented various protocols, including lockdowns, social distancing, and the widespread use of contact tracing. However, the effectiveness of these measures relies heavily on the accuracy of the information provided by the public. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop a system that can detect misinformation and rumors to prevent the spread of false narratives. This paper introduces a novel dual-stage categorization framework designed to identify misinformation by leveraging BERT attributes. The approach first employs a BERT-based dual-stage method to classify news content, followed by a second stage that utilizes BERT attributes to pinpoint specific false elements within the text. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in identifying misinformation.

This paper introduces a curated list of resources designed to support network researchers, particularly those early in their careers. We categorize these materials into three groups: foundational, applied, and advanced. The foundational resources cover core concepts and models, while applied resources focus on tools and methods for data analysis. Advanced resources include cutting-edge research directions and emerging technologies. We believe this "atlas" will be valuable to anyone seeking to navigate the complex landscape of network research.

Time is a critical factor in eco-evolutionary dynamics, yet the mechanisms governing its influence remain unclear. This study examines how time interacts with population dynamics in a system featuring a predator and a prey that can evolve resistance. We identify two primary drivers: the speed at which resistance evolves and the magnitude of its effect on predator mortality. By analyzing the system's long-term behavior, we demonstrate that temporal impacts are dictated by two mechanisms: (1) the system's proximity to a long-term evolutionary stable state (ESS) and (2) the degree of divergence between initial and long-term outcomes. Furthermore, we show that the evolution of time-dependent impacts stems from the combined action of two processes: (1) the disparity between short-term and long-term dynamics, and (2) the frequency of oscillations in population levels. These findings offer a theoretical framework for understanding temporal dynamics within eco-evolutionary contexts.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a standard approach for speech representation extraction, typically involving the creation of pre-trained models on vast datasets before fine-tuning on smaller, task-specific ones. Despite the success of these models, their resilience to adversarial attacks remains underexplored. This study investigates the susceptibility of SSL to such attacks, revealing that while they are more resistant than traditional discriminative models, significant vulnerabilities persist. We introduce a novel metric to quantify this susceptibility and demonstrate that it correlates with the model's classification entropy. Furthermore, we find that these attacks can severely compromise SSL performance across various downstream tasks, including speaker identification and emotion recognition. Finally, we explore mitigation strategies, showing that retraining on larger datasets and employing adversarial training can substantially improve robustness.

The decentralized economy is a peer-to-peer framework where individuals and organizations can directly exchange goods and services without reliance on centralized intermediaries. Blockchain technology serves as a vital foundation for this model, offering an immutable ledger, transparent record-keeping, and automated smart contracts. This paper examines the integration of blockchain within decentralized marketplaces, analyzing the advantages of this convergence alongside the associated hurdles. Furthermore, it outlines the essential characteristics required for building blockchain-enabled marketplaces and provides an overview of pioneering use cases. The discussion concludes with an exploration of future research avenues and prospective developments in this domain.

Sensitivity analysis is essential when dealing with missing data, as it assesses how robust study conclusions remain under various untestable assumptions. Recently, the E‑value has emerged as a metric for quantifying the robustness of causal inferences drawn from randomized trials. This study introduces a method for calculating E‑values in the context of missing data, demonstrating its utility through a simulation framework. The proposed approach is illustrated using data from the Women's Health Initiative, which examined the link between hormone therapy and coronary heart disease.
